title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 22
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Written-Off Car
listeningScripts.text: Caller: My car was written off after the accident, and the insurer has offered eight thousand two hundred. I can't replace it for that. Adviser: Let me take some details. Make, model, year? Caller: A twenty-eighteen estate, seventy-nine thousand kilometres, one owner. Adviser: And is the eight thousand two hundred described as a market value, or as a settlement offer? Caller: Market value. Adviser: Right. That is their estimate of what the car was worth the day before the accident, and it is an estimate you are allowed to argue with. Most people don't, which is why first offers are what they are. Caller: How do I argue with it? Adviser: Evidence, not opinion. Three advertisements for the same model, same year, similar kilometres, from within the last thirty days, in your region. Screenshots with the date visible. Not what you paid, and not what you think it is worth. What the same car is selling for now. Caller: There are four on the dealer sites at eleven and a half. Adviser: Then that is your case, although I would temper the expectation. A dealer's asking price sits above a private sale, and the insurer will discount it. If the advertisements average eleven and a half, a realistic landing point is nine and a half to ten. Caller: How long do I have? Adviser: Fourteen days from the offer. And this is the part that matters: accepting the offer ends it. Don't accept while you are still gathering evidence, even if the money would be useful now. Caller: And if they refuse? Adviser: Then it goes to the ombudsman, which is free and takes about eight weeks. But you have to have disputed it with the insurer in writing first. The ombudsman won't look at anything the insurer hasn't had a chance to answer.

listeningScripts.title: The Tree on the Boundary
listeningScripts.text: A: Can I ask you about the sycamore? B: I knew this was coming. Go on. A: It isn't a complaint. It's that half of it is over my side now, and it takes the light off the back of the house from about two o'clock. B: I can't afford to take it down. I looked into it. Eighteen hundred with the stump. A: I'm not asking you to take it down. I like the tree. I'm asking about the three branches on my side. B: You're allowed to cut those. That's the law, isn't it? Anything overhanging your boundary. A: You are, but you have to offer the cuttings back, which is the silliest rule in the country, and I would rather ask you first than exercise a right at you. B: Appreciated. What would it cost to do just the three? A: Four hundred, and I'll pay it, because it's my light. B: Then split it. It's my tree and it has got too big, and I would rather it were pruned properly than have you doing it off a ladder. A: Two hundred each, then. One more thing. It has a preservation order, so the work needs notice to the council six weeks ahead. B: Six weeks. So that's March, not January. A: March. Which is the right time to prune it anyway.

listeningScripts.title: Day Surgery Pre-Admission
listeningScripts.text: Right. You are booked for Thursday the fourteenth, and this is the pre-admission call. I will go through six things and then you can ask me anything. Eating and drinking. No food from midnight. Clear fluids — water, black tea, apple juice, nothing with milk and nothing with pulp — until two hours before you arrive, so that is until half past five. The two-hour rule is newer than people expect. If a relative tells you nothing at all after midnight, they are remembering an older instruction, and being dehydrated makes the cannula harder, not easier. Medication. Everything as normal except blood thinners, and yours stop on the Monday. That is already on your file, but say it back to me if you can. Diabetes medication has its own sheet and I will post that to you. You need somebody to take you home and stay the night. Not a taxi. We will cancel on the day if there is no named adult, and I know that sounds harsh, but the anaesthetic does not clear for twenty-four hours, and people fall. Bring your ordinary glasses rather than contact lenses, and leave jewellery at home. A wedding ring is fine — we tape it. Arrival is half past seven, and your procedure is not at half past seven. The order of the list is decided by the anaesthetist on the morning, and it depends on who needs what. You may be first and you may be fourth. Bring something to read, and expect to be with us most of the day. And if you develop a cold before Thursday, ring us. Don't simply turn up and hope. A chest infection with an anaesthetic is the one thing we will not work around.

listeningScripts.title: Alternate-Day Letter Delivery
listeningScripts.text: Canada Post will move to alternate-day letter delivery in three cities from September, in a trial the corporation describes as a response to a fall of more than sixty per cent in letter volumes since two thousand and six. Under the trial, addresses will receive letters every second working day rather than daily. Parcels are unaffected and will continue to be delivered six days a week, which the corporation says reflects where the volume and the revenue now are. The three cities have not been named. The corporation said they will be chosen to give a mix of urban and suburban routes, and will be announced before the end of June. The postal union opposed the trial, arguing that it is a step towards permanent reduction rather than a genuine experiment, and that the savings estimate of ninety million a year assumes a route consolidation that would cut about six hundred positions. The corporation disputed the job figure, but confirmed that no route consolidation decisions will be taken until the trial has run for a full year. Small business groups were divided. Those that send invoices objected; those that mostly receive parcels were indifferent.

listeningScripts.title: Short-Term Subletting in the Co-op
listeningScripts.text: Raghunathan: The proposal is to allow members to sublet for up to sixty days a year, with notice to the board. Oyelowo: Sixty days is two months. That isn't a member who is away. That's a business. Raghunathan: It's a member who works a contract in Yellowknife for two months — which is Priya — and who currently either pays double rent or breaks the rules. Oyelowo: Then write it for that. Sixty consecutive days, once a year, with the reason stated. Not sixty days scattered through the year in weekends, because that is a different activity with the same number attached to it. Lindqvist: That distinction is enforceable, which most of them are not. I can check consecutive. Raghunathan: What about insurance? Lindqvist: Our policy covers a member's guests. It does not cover a paying occupant, and the difference matters if there is a fire. A member subletting without telling us is uninsured and doesn't know it. Oyelowo: That's an argument for the rule, then, not against it. At the moment people do it anyway and we don't know. Lindqvist: Which is why I'm in favour. I would rather have a register than a rumour. Raghunathan: And the neighbours? Oyelowo: The complaint is never the subletting. It's not knowing who is in the building. If the rule requires the subtenant's name given to the board and the two adjacent units notified, most of the objection goes away. Lindqvist: I can administer that. Two units either side, by email, before the tenancy starts. Raghunathan: Then I'll redraft it as consecutive days, once yearly, with notification. Same sixty.

listeningScripts.title: Abolishing the Clock Change
listeningScripts.text: Almost everybody agrees that the clock change should stop. Almost nobody agrees on what should replace it, and that disagreement is the reason nothing has happened in twenty years. There are two ways to stop changing the clocks, and they are not the same policy. Permanent daylight time gives you a later sunset all year, and a very late winter sunrise — in the northern part of this country, past nine o'clock in December. Permanent standard time gives you an earlier winter sunrise and a summer sunset that arrives before many people have finished work. Polling reliably prefers permanent daylight time, by large margins. Sleep researchers reliably prefer permanent standard time, also by large margins. That is not the usual pattern, where experts and the public disagree because the public has not read the studies. It is a genuine difference in what is being valued. The public is answering a question about summer evenings. The researchers are answering a question about winter mornings and circadian alignment. The historical evidence is worth knowing. Permanent daylight time has been tried, in the United States in nineteen seventy-four, during an energy crisis. It was repealed within ten months, and the thing that killed it was children going to school in the dark in January. That is an argument which polls badly in June and decisively in January. So my position is permanent standard time, held with less confidence than I would like, and a strong recommendation that any jurisdiction doing this moves at the same time as its neighbours. Being an hour out from the province next door is worse than either option.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: Her insurer has refused to write the car off
The offer for her written-off car is too low to replace it
She has been charged for a repair she did not authorise
Her insurance was cancelled after the accident
questions.correctAnswer: The offer for her written-off car is too low to replace it
questions.explanation: The car was written off and the insurer offered eight thousand two hundred, which the caller says will not replace it.

questions.prompt: What does a market value figure represent?
options: The price the caller originally paid
The amount the insurer is obliged to pay
The cost of repairing the car
The insurer's estimate of the car's worth the day before the accident
questions.correctAnswer: The insurer's estimate of the car's worth the day before the accident
questions.explanation: Market value is the insurer's estimate of the pre-accident worth — an estimate the adviser says the caller is entitled to argue with.

questions.prompt: Why does the adviser say first offers are what they are?
options: They are set by an independent assessor
They allow for the cost of a hire car
Most people do not argue with them
They are calculated from a national average
questions.correctAnswer: Most people do not argue with them
questions.explanation: The adviser's explanation is behavioural: the figure is an estimate that can be challenged, and most people simply do not challenge it.

questions.prompt: What evidence does the adviser ask for?
options: Three recent local advertisements for the same model
A valuation from an independent garage
The original purchase receipt
A written statement of the car's condition
questions.correctAnswer: Three recent local advertisements for the same model
questions.explanation: Three advertisements for the same model and year with similar kilometres, from the last thirty days and in her region, screenshotted with the date visible.

questions.prompt: What does the adviser say about dealer prices?
options: They are the only evidence an insurer accepts
The insurer will discount them, because a dealer asks more than a private sale
They are usually lower than private sale prices
They cannot be used if the car is over five years old
questions.correctAnswer: The insurer will discount them, because a dealer asks more than a private sale
questions.explanation: A dealer's asking price sits above a private sale, so the insurer will discount it — which is why the adviser tempers the expectation.

questions.prompt: What outcome does the adviser call realistic?
options: Between nine and a half and ten thousand
Eleven and a half thousand
Eight thousand two hundred
Whatever the ombudsman decides
questions.correctAnswer: Between nine and a half and ten thousand
questions.explanation: With advertisements averaging eleven and a half, the adviser puts a realistic landing point at nine and a half to ten thousand.

questions.prompt: Why must the caller not accept the offer yet?
options: The fourteen days have not started
The evidence must be sent first
A second offer is due automatically
Accepting it ends the dispute
questions.correctAnswer: Accepting it ends the dispute
questions.explanation: Acceptance closes the matter, so the adviser warns against accepting while evidence is still being gathered, however useful the money would be now.

questions.prompt: What has to happen before the ombudsman will look at it?
options: Fourteen days must pass from the offer
An independent valuation must be obtained
The dispute must be put to the insurer in writing
The insurer must agree to the referral
questions.correctAnswer: The dispute must be put to the insurer in writing
questions.explanation: The ombudsman is free and takes about eight weeks, but will not consider anything the insurer has not had a chance to answer in writing.

questions.prompt: What is A's difficulty with the tree?
options: The back of the house loses its afternoon light
Its roots are lifting A's patio
Its branches are close to A's roof
Its leaves block A's gutters
questions.correctAnswer: The back of the house loses its afternoon light
questions.explanation: A is careful to say it is not a complaint: half the tree is now over A's side and it takes the light from about two o'clock.

questions.prompt: What has B assumed A is asking for?
options: That B pay for a survey
That the boundary be moved
That the tree be taken down
That A be allowed to plant something else
questions.correctAnswer: That the tree be taken down
questions.explanation: B's first response is about affording to take it down at eighteen hundred with the stump, which A immediately corrects — A likes the tree.

questions.prompt: What does A say must be done when cutting overhanging branches?
options: The neighbour's written permission is needed
The council must inspect the work first
The cutting must be done in winter
The cuttings have to be offered back
questions.correctAnswer: The cuttings have to be offered back
questions.explanation: A confirms the right to cut what overhangs, but points out the obligation to offer the cuttings back — and would rather ask than exercise a right at a neighbour.

questions.prompt: Why does B offer to split the cost?
options: B accepts that the tree is too close to the boundary
B would rather the tree were pruned properly
B wants the work done before March
The council would otherwise charge B
questions.correctAnswer: B would rather the tree were pruned properly
questions.explanation: B's reason is the tree itself: it is B's, it has grown too big, and B prefers proper pruning to A working off a ladder.

questions.prompt: Why must the work wait until March?
options: A tree survey has to be carried out first
The contractor has no availability before March
B cannot afford it until then
A preservation order requires six weeks' notice to the council
questions.correctAnswer: A preservation order requires six weeks' notice to the council
questions.explanation: The preservation order means six weeks' notice to the council, which pushes the work from January to March — which A notes is the right time to prune anyway.

questions.prompt: Until when may clear fluids be taken?
options: Until midnight
Until half past seven
Until two hours before arrival, at half past five
Until the procedure begins
questions.correctAnswer: Until two hours before arrival, at half past five
questions.explanation: Food stops at midnight, but clear fluids are allowed until two hours before arrival — half past five for a half past seven arrival.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker mention dehydration?
options: Being dehydrated makes the cannula harder to place
It increases the risk of infection
It delays the anaesthetic taking effect
It means the procedure has to be rescheduled
questions.correctAnswer: Being dehydrated makes the cannula harder to place
questions.explanation: The two-hour rule is newer than people expect, and a relative's older advice to take nothing after midnight leaves patients dehydrated, which makes the cannula harder rather than easier.

questions.prompt: Which medication stops on the Monday?
options: The diabetes medication
The blood thinners
All regular medication
Nothing stops before the procedure
questions.correctAnswer: The blood thinners
questions.explanation: Everything continues as normal except the blood thinners, which stop on the Monday; diabetes medication has its own sheet, which will be posted.

questions.prompt: Why must somebody stay overnight?
options: The hospital cannot discharge a patient alone
A district nurse cannot visit until morning
The dressing has to be changed at night
The anaesthetic takes twenty-four hours to clear and people fall
questions.correctAnswer: The anaesthetic takes twenty-four hours to clear and people fall
questions.explanation: A named adult must take the patient home and stay the night — not a taxi — because the anaesthetic does not clear for twenty-four hours and people fall.

questions.prompt: Why is the arrival time not the time of the procedure?
options: Emergencies are always treated first
The ward opens before the theatre does
The anaesthetist decides the order of the list that morning
Patients are seen in the order they arrive
questions.correctAnswer: The anaesthetist decides the order of the list that morning
questions.explanation: Everyone arrives at half past seven, and the anaesthetist sets the order on the morning according to who needs what — so a patient may be first or fourth.

questions.prompt: What should a patient do who develops a cold?
options: Telephone the hospital rather than simply attending
Attend as booked and mention it on arrival
Cancel the appointment and rebook online
Take a decongestant on the morning
questions.correctAnswer: Telephone the hospital rather than simply attending
questions.explanation: The instruction is to ring rather than turn up and hope, because a chest infection with an anaesthetic is the one thing the department will not work around.

questions.prompt: What is changing?
options: Letters will no longer be delivered in three cities
Parcel delivery will be reduced to three days
Delivery will stop on Saturdays nationwide
Letters will arrive every second working day in three cities
questions.correctAnswer: Letters will arrive every second working day in three cities
questions.explanation: The trial moves three cities to alternate-day letter delivery from September, with letters arriving every second working day rather than daily.

questions.prompt: What reason does the corporation give?
options: Letter volumes have fallen by more than sixty per cent
Parcel volumes have doubled since two thousand and six
Three cities requested the change
Staff numbers have fallen faster than expected
questions.correctAnswer: Letter volumes have fallen by more than sixty per cent
questions.explanation: The corporation frames the trial as a response to letter volumes falling more than sixty per cent since two thousand and six.

questions.prompt: What is not affected?
options: Letters to businesses
Parcels, which continue six days a week
Deliveries in suburban areas
Mail sent between the three cities
questions.correctAnswer: Parcels, which continue six days a week
questions.explanation: Parcels are unaffected and stay on six-day delivery, which the corporation says is where the volume and the revenue now are.

questions.prompt: What does the postal union argue?
options: The savings estimate is too small to justify it
The three cities were chosen unfairly
The trial is a step towards a permanent reduction
Parcels should be reduced instead of letters
questions.correctAnswer: The trial is a step towards a permanent reduction
questions.explanation: The union's objection is that this is not a genuine experiment but a step towards permanent reduction, and that the ninety-million saving assumes a consolidation cutting about six hundred positions.

questions.prompt: What did the corporation confirm?
options: No consolidation decisions until the trial has run a year
That six hundred positions will go
That the trial will be extended to more cities
That the cities will be named in September
questions.correctAnswer: No consolidation decisions until the trial has run a year
questions.explanation: The corporation disputed the six-hundred figure but confirmed that no route consolidation decisions will be taken until the trial has run for a full year.

questions.prompt: What does the proposal allow?
options: Subletting for up to two months without notice
Subletting for up to sixty days a year, with notice to the board
Subletting only to other members of the co-op
Subletting for any period, subject to a fee
questions.correctAnswer: Subletting for up to sixty days a year, with notice to the board
questions.explanation: Raghunathan's proposal is sixty days a year with notice to the board, which the discussion then reshapes.

questions.prompt: What is Oyelowo's objection?
options: Sixty days is too short to be useful
Members would sublet to strangers
The board could not refuse an application
Sixty days spread through the year describes a business
questions.correctAnswer: Sixty days spread through the year describes a business
questions.explanation: Oyelowo's point is that sixty days is two months, and that scattered weekends adding to sixty are a different activity with the same number attached.

questions.prompt: What does Oyelowo propose instead?
options: Thirty days a year with no reason required
Sixty days limited to members working away
Sixty consecutive days, once a year, with the reason given
A ban on subletting with an exception for Priya
questions.correctAnswer: Sixty consecutive days, once a year, with the reason given
questions.explanation: Oyelowo would write the rule for the case it was meant for: sixty consecutive days, once a year, with the reason stated.

questions.prompt: Why does Lindqvist support that wording?
options: Consecutive days can actually be checked
It matches the insurer's requirements
It reduces the administrative work
It is what other co-ops have adopted
questions.correctAnswer: Consecutive days can actually be checked
questions.explanation: Lindqvist's reason is enforceability: unlike most such distinctions, consecutive days is something the office can verify.

questions.prompt: What is the insurance position?
options: The policy covers subletting if the board approves it
The policy covers a member's guests but not a paying occupant
Subletting voids the policy for the whole building
A separate policy is required for every tenancy
questions.correctAnswer: The policy covers a member's guests but not a paying occupant
questions.explanation: The co-op's policy covers guests, not paying occupants, and the difference matters in a fire — so a member subletting quietly is uninsured without realising it.

questions.prompt: Why does Oyelowo say that argues for the rule?
options: People sublet anyway, and the co-op does not know who is uninsured
The insurer has asked for a written policy
A rule would allow the co-op to charge for cover
Members would otherwise be evicted
questions.correctAnswer: People sublet anyway, and the co-op does not know who is uninsured
questions.explanation: Oyelowo turns the insurance point around: the risk exists already because people sublet unrecorded, so a rule that brings it into the open reduces it.

questions.prompt: What does Oyelowo say the neighbours actually object to?
options: Noise from short-term occupants
The loss of parking spaces
Not knowing who is in the building
Members profiting from co-op housing
questions.correctAnswer: Not knowing who is in the building
questions.explanation: Oyelowo says the complaint is never the subletting itself but not knowing who is in the building — which naming the subtenant and notifying the adjacent units largely answers.

questions.prompt: What will Lindqvist administer?
options: Collecting a deposit from each subtenant
Inspecting the unit after each tenancy
Keeping the register confidential from neighbours
Emailing the two units either side before the tenancy starts
questions.correctAnswer: Emailing the two units either side before the tenancy starts
questions.explanation: Lindqvist undertakes the notification: the two units either side, by email, before the tenancy begins.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say nothing has happened in twenty years?
options: There is no agreement on what should replace the clock change
Governments have not been asked to act
The evidence has only recently been gathered
Neighbouring jurisdictions have refused to co-operate
questions.correctAnswer: There is no agreement on what should replace the clock change
questions.explanation: Almost everybody agrees the change should stop; the deadlock is over which of the two replacements to adopt.

questions.prompt: What does permanent daylight time produce?
options: Earlier sunsets and earlier sunrises
Later sunsets in summer only
A shorter winter day overall
Later sunsets all year and a very late winter sunrise
questions.correctAnswer: Later sunsets all year and a very late winter sunrise
questions.explanation: Permanent daylight time gives a later sunset all year and a winter sunrise that, in the north of the country, arrives after nine in December.

questions.prompt: How do polling and researchers differ?
options: The public is evenly split while researchers are not
The public prefers permanent daylight time and researchers permanent standard
Researchers prefer keeping the clock change
Both prefer permanent daylight time
questions.correctAnswer: The public prefers permanent daylight time and researchers permanent standard
questions.explanation: Polling reliably favours permanent daylight time by large margins, and sleep researchers reliably favour permanent standard time, also by large margins.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say this is not the usual expert-public disagreement?
options: The public has read the studies in this case
The researchers disagree among themselves
The two groups are valuing different things
Both sides are relying on the same evidence
questions.correctAnswer: The two groups are valuing different things
questions.explanation: This is not a case of the public not having read the studies: the public is answering a question about summer evenings and the researchers one about winter mornings and circadian alignment.

questions.prompt: What ended the nineteen seventy-four experiment?
options: Children going to school in the dark
The end of the energy crisis
A change of government
Evidence about sleep and health
questions.correctAnswer: Children going to school in the dark
questions.explanation: Permanent daylight time was repealed within ten months, and what killed it was children going to school in the dark in January — an argument that polls badly in June and decisively in January.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker recommend alongside their preferred option?
options: Holding a referendum before any change
Trialling the change for a single winter
Moving at the same time as neighbouring jurisdictions
Leaving the decision to individual cities
questions.correctAnswer: Moving at the same time as neighbouring jurisdictions
questions.explanation: The speaker holds for permanent standard time with less confidence than they would like, and recommends strongly that any jurisdiction move together with its neighbours, since being an hour out from the province next door is worse than either option.
